metadata.description: One Measured Chain recipe per project-created task per chip target, and the one home of every Recorded Chain (ADR 0040, amended 2026-09-27)
metadata.rule: stack = ceil_512(ceil(chain * 1.25)); in integer arithmetic, need = (chain * 5 + 3) // 4, stack = ((need + 511) // 512) * 512
notes: Fifteen tasks: the eleven created in src/main.cpp, plus the PCA9685's sender (src/drivers/pca9685.cpp, started only when that expander is the chosen body servo controller and answers), WebEvents and the ArduinoOTA task (src/web/web_server.cpp) and HostedRecovery (src/web/web_network_manager_hosted.cpp). HostedRecovery exists only where PA_CAP_HOSTED_WIFI is 1, so artoo-esp32 has fourteen and the ESP32-P4 fifteen.
loopTask is sized by ARDUINO_LOOP_STACK_SIZE in platformio.ini and is deliberately outside this table.

Per arm: 'chain_bytes' is the Recorded Chain, the walk of the image 'env' names; 'stack_bytes' is the task's stack. Whether the stack is on the rule, above it or declines it is derived from those two every time it is needed and never stored. 'reason' says why wherever the stack is not what the rule gives, and 'note' says why the chain is as deep as it is today - the history of a figure is the git log's. include/task_stack_figures.h is generated from this file and include/config.h includes it.

Figures are written by a command, not by hand: tools/check_task_stack_chains.py --rewrite --chip <esp32|esp32p4> builds the chip's product image, records every walked chain, prints the stack the rule wants against each 'stack_bytes' with what taking it costs, and changes a stack only with --accept. It then regenerates the header; test/test_tools/test_task_stack_figures_drift.py fails when the two disagree.

'env' is always the chip's product image ('envs' below). Where the product image emits a body as data, an arm may name another image that decodes it; that arm is then neither checked nor rewritten against the product image, and says so on the gate row.

chain = max over 'roots' of that root's total worst-case chain, plus the sum of the own frames named in 'frames'. A frame is stitched by hand only where the walker cannot follow the call that reaches it (an indirect call through a function pointer); 'stitch_reason' says which call and why. An indirect call BELOW a root, through a pointer read from a dispatch table, is stitched by 'tables': every function the named table holds in the image becomes a callee of 'caller', so the walk itself takes the deepest row and a row added later is walked without editing this file (#429).

Every figure is a floor: indirect calls that are not stitched are not followed, and call-graph cycles are cut. On artoo-esp32 objdump prints a third of the function bodies as data, because the linked image keeps only part of its .xt.prop property table and objdump decodes an address in a gap between records by the NEXT record's flags (#430); tools/stack_usage_report.py decodes those bodies from a copy of the image without .xt.prop/.xt.lit, taking only them from it, and the gate row counts the bodies recovered and any still printed as data, whose frames read as zero. The ESP32-P4 image decodes whole. So a chain can be missed and cannot be overstated, which is what makes the re-walk safe to fail a build on.

The walk is bounded: tools/stack_usage_report.py reads each function body to its ELF symbol size rather than to the next symbol objdump prints, so a literal-pool word that decodes as a call to a real entry is not followed, and relinking identical source cannot move a chain (#271).

'pointer_calls' (top level, not per task) stitches a function pointer the program sets at run time and a library calls through from several places: every function the listing shows loading 'pointer' and calling indirectly becomes a caller of each of 'callees', on every chip in 'chips', for every task (stack_usage_report.Image.stitch_pointer_calls(), #430). The callers are found, not listed, so a library update that adds one is walked without editing this file, and a pointer nothing calls through any more fails the gate row.

The IDF log hook is why chains differ most between the chips. artoo-esp32 links newlib nano printf, so the hook's formatting is shallow there; the ESP32-P4 keeps full newlib, so wherever a task can reach an ESP-IDF log call its chain carries the RISC-V vsnprintf float tail, whose _svfprintf_r and _dtoa_r frames are far wider than on Xtensa (#245, #430).

'infeasible_calls' (top level, not per task) removes call edges the listing shows but that cannot execute, each with its reason and the two sites that prove it: the call and the caller that makes it impossible. Removing an edge can only lower a walk, so every entry is evidence the operator can check, not a convenience; an entry whose edge is no longer in the image fails the gate row (stack_usage_report.Image.drop_infeasible_calls(), #430).

Interrupt and exception frames are not counted: both ports spill some state to the interrupted task's stack before switching to the ISR stack. The rule's 25% is what covers that, so an arm that declines the rule has less cover for it than one that does not.

pointer_calls.reason: src/main.cpp paLogInit() installs paLogIdfVprintf with esp_log_set_vprintf(), which stores it in esp_log_vprint_func (ESP-IDF components/log/src/os/log_write.c). Every ESP-IDF log line is printed through that pointer: esp_log_va() calls it (log.c, CONFIG_LOG_VERSION=1 on both chips) and so does esp_log(), into which the compiler inlines the same call; esp_log_writev() and esp_log_write() reach it through esp_log_va(). The hook formats into a PA_LOG_SERIAL_LINE_MAX buffer on the calling task's stack and runs paLogLine(), 2544 B on artoo-esp32 (#428), so a task that reaches any ESP-IDF log call carries it. At #430 both images call through the pointer from esp_log_va and esp_log only; esp_log_set_vprintf stores it and makes no call. On both chips since #430 (2026-09-26): on artoo-esp32 newlib nano printf pays for it and every chain still fits its stack; on the ESP32-P4, which keeps full newlib, the stacks were raised by the allocation rule to cover it (operator decision 2026-09-26).

infeasible_calls.call_site: ESP-IDF components/esp_mm/esp_cache_msync.c:281, the first line of esp_cache_get_alignment(): ESP_RETURN_ON_FALSE(out_alignment, ESP_ERR_INVALID_ARG, TAG, "null pointer"). Its ESP_LOGE is the esp_log_timestamp() and esp_log() calls, both on line 281 in the listing.
infeasible_calls.proof_site: Every caller in the linked images passes the address of a local, which is never null. artoo_esp32 has one caller: ESP-IDF components/esp_mm/heap_align_hw.c:54, esp_heap_adjust_alignment_to_hw(), esp_cache_get_alignment(caps, &cache_alignment_bytes). firebeetle2 has that one and components/esp_driver_sdmmc/src/sdmmc_host.c:1304, sdmmc_host_check_buffer_alignment(), esp_cache_get_alignment(cache_flags, &cache_alignment_bytes). Callers counted from each image's listing at #430; a new caller must be read before this entry is trusted again.
infeasible_calls.reason: Every malloc in the image reaches esp_cache_get_alignment() through heap_caps_aligned_alloc_base -> esp_heap_adjust_alignment_to_hw, so this one log statement sat under every task. With the IDF log hook stitched it carried the hook onto eleven of twelve artoo-esp32 chains, and it is also the 'ESP-IDF log/queue tail below esp_cache_get_alignment()' include/config.h names under AudioTask. It cannot run (#430).

esp32.stitch_reason: This task carries out an operator-requested restart (#428), and esp_restart() runs every handler registered with esp_register_shutdown_handler() on the calling task, through a pointer array filled at run time. This image registers two: esp_sync_timekeeping_timers (esp_timer's system_time.c, because both CONFIG_ESP_TIME_FUNCS_USE_ESP_TIMER and _RTC_TIMER are set) and esp_wifi_stop (esp_wifi's wifi_default.c:273). libbt's handler is not linked (CONFIG_BT_ENABLED=n) and the Arduino core's usb_persist_shutdown_handler is registered only by usb_persist_restart(), which nothing calls. esp_wifi_stop is libnet80211.a's (ieee80211_api.o) and objdump emits its body in this image as data, so it and every closed body it reaches are walked from their archive members; the closed code calls the OS adapter through g_osi_funcs_p, which esp_wifi_init() points at g_wifi_osi_funcs at run time. esp_wifi_stop's error paths reach the IDF log hook, which the top-level pointer_calls entry walks.

The root frame is the same inlined one as the artoo-esp32 arm: the ServoOutputRow and ServoCommandedPosition of centreOneOutput() and the boot pass's owed-release check, the Gesture run's intake, and since #453 the Cadence Floor each inlined run reads from the config cache, which took it from 656 B to 672 B and the chain from 6112 B to 6128 B. The flutter run and the flutter request's intake are out of line with their state in statics and are not on this route. 6128 B is 20 B short of the rule step (6128 -> 7660 of 7680): the next 32 B on this route is a stack decision. At #444 the root frame walked 656 B, 16 B less, with nothing in this task's own source changed.

esp32.stitch_reason: embedded-cli reaches the command callback through `cli->onCommand`, a call through a function pointer that the walker does not follow, so the chain has to be stitched from its two halves: onCliCommand's total plus the two frames above it. embeddedCliProcess's frame already contains parseCommand and onControlInput, which GCC inlines into it - both are ABSENT as symbols, which is what confirms it rather than a missing measurement. Below the root, consoleExecuteCommand runs a status or api op through `executor(request->requestId, sink)` (src/console/console_module.cpp), a pointer read from g_statusExecutors, so every row of that table is stitched as a callee (#429). A direct action and an audio config write are reached the same way, through a pointer found in one of the six g_*DirectActionExecutors tables or g_audioConfigExecutors, so those rows are stitched too (#428). A single-field Setting op and aux.config.led-count are direct calls since #431, which the walker follows without a stitch. Without it the recorded chain could not include an op's frame, which is how the ESP32-P4 overflow under consoleExecuteDomeApiGetSequenceLastRun (#427) stayed invisible.
